raw.reply: You’ll usually choose between two main Medicare paths: Original Medicare, which is Parts A and B from the federal program, or a Medicare Advantage plan, which provides Parts A and B through a private plan. With Original Medicare, you can add a separate drug plan and may be able to buy Medigap; with Medicare Advantage, drug coverage is included in most plans, and you still pay the Part B premium either way.
raw.question: What health insurance do you have now?

Birthday, desired start, job end, insurance end and actual enrollment are distinct.

Unknown, deferred, none, tentative and stale are distinct; do not invent missing precision.

evidence.title: What Medicare is
evidence.text: Medicare is health insurance from the federal government. It helps pay for health care. It is mainly for people 65 or older who meet the program’s eligibility rules. Some younger people qualify because of a disability, End-Stage Renal Disease, or ALS. You can learn the coverage pieces one at a time.
evidence.summary: Medicare is federal health insurance. We’ll build the rest of the picture one piece at a time.
evidence.question: What is Medicare?

evidence.title: The two parts to start with
evidence.text:
Part A: Hospital insurance: inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facility care, hospice and some home health care.

Part B: Medical insurance: doctors, outpatient care, tests, equipment and many preventive services.

Parts A and B together, run by the federal government and accepted by any U.S. doctor who takes Medicare.
evidence.summary: Part A is hospital insurance. Part B is medical insurance. Together, they are Original Medicare.
evidence.question: What do Parts A and B cover?

evidence.title: The two coverage routes
evidence.text: Original Medicare is Parts A and B through the federal program. Medicare Advantage is a private plan approved by Medicare that provides Parts A and B. Both routes provide Medicare coverage, with different rules and costs. We can add the other coverage pieces after this distinction is clear.
evidence.summary: You can get Parts A and B through the federal program or through a private Medicare Advantage plan.
evidence.question: What are the two ways to get Medicare?

evidence.title: How your options fit together
evidence.text: There are two main routes. Original Medicare is Parts A and B; you can add a separate drug plan and may be able to buy Medigap to help with your share of costs. Medicare Advantage provides A and B through a private plan, and most plans include drug coverage. Medigap goes with Original Medicare, not Medicare Advantage. You still pay the Part B premium with either route.
evidence.summary: Start with hospital and medical care. Then compare the two ways to get your coverage.
evidence.question: How do my Medicare options fit together?

evidence.title: Dates depend on your situation
evidence.text: A birthday and current work coverage do not establish when Part B actually starts. Social Security confirms the enrollment route and effective date. Unknown dates stay unknown. The timeline uses the facts entered in this tab. An unknown date stays an open check; special enrollment rights may need separate confirmation.
evidence.summary: Your birth date, actual coverage, and job insurance can affect which dates need checking.
evidence.question: Why do these dates matter?

evidence.title: What to check for each plan
evidence.text: Records are in source order or ordered by explicit published fields. Eligibility, doctor participation, exact medicines and personal total cost have not been established. Compare the exact plan's providers, drug coverage, costs, and enrollment requirements before making a decision.
evidence.summary: A plan list is the starting point. Check doctors, medicines, and costs for your situation.
evidence.question: What should I check before choosing a plan?

evidence.title: Getting started with enrollment timing
evidence.question: How does first Medicare enrollment timing work?
evidence.text: For most people first becoming eligible at 65, the Initial Enrollment Period is a 7-month window: the 3 months before the birthday month, that month, and the 3 months after. The date coverage begins also depends on when enrollment happens and which enrollment period applies. Current health insurance matters: Medicare.gov checks the kind of insurance, whether job-based coverage comes from current employment, and employer size before giving timing guidance. Do not turn this general explanation into a personal start date, deadline, eligibility decision or permission to delay Part B. A first-of-month birthday has special start-date rules.
evidence.summary: The sign-up window and coverage start are different; current insurance helps identify the relevant timing questions.
